before: When an accident leaves you unable to work, the financial pressure starts almost immediately. Bills keep coming. Rent is still due. Your employer may hold your position for a while, but your paycheck stops the moment you do. If someone else caused your injury, Georgia and South Carolina law both allow you to recover the wages you lost — and in many cases, the income you will lose in the future. According to the Cornell Law Institute, compensatory damages in personal injury cases include both economic losses like lost wages and non-economic losses like pain and suffering. Understanding how lost wage claims work in each state is the first step toward getting the compensation you actually deserve.
after: When an accident leaves you unable to work, the financial pressure starts almost immediately. Bills keep coming. Rent is still due. Your employer may hold your position for a while, but your paycheck stops the moment you do. If someone else caused your injury, Georgia and South Carolina law both allow you to recover the wages you lost — and in many cases, the income you will lose in the future. According to the Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute, compensatory damages in personal injury cases include both economic losses like lost wages and non-economic losses like pain and suffering. Understanding how lost wage claims work in each state is the first step toward getting the compensation you actually deserve.

before:
Lost wages cover more than just your base salary or hourly pay. Georgia and South Carolina courts recognize several categories of lost income in personal injury claims:

  • Base salary or hourly wages — Your regular pay for the hours or days you missed
  • Overtime pay — If you regularly worked overtime before the accident, you can claim the overtime you would have earned
  • Bonuses and commissions — Performance bonuses, sales commissions, and incentive pay you lost due to being unable to work
  • Tips and gratuities — For restaurant workers, bartenders, valets, and others who rely on tips as a substantial part of their income
  • Vacation and sick days used — If you burned through your PTO or sick leave to cover your recovery period, those days have a cash value
  • Benefits lost — Health insurance contributions, retirement plan matches, stock options, and other employer-provided benefits
  • Promotion opportunities missed — If you were in line for a promotion or raise that you lost because of your absence
  • Self-employment income — Business profits you would have earned if you could have continued working

The key principle is that you should be made whole. Whatever income the accident took from you — directly or indirectly — is recoverable if you can prove it. This applies whether your injuries came from a car accident, a trucking collision, or a construction site incident.
after:
Lost wages cover more than just your base salary or hourly pay. Georgia and South Carolina let you recover any earnings the injury cost you, as long as you can prove the amount with reasonable certainty. In practice that can include:

  • Base salary or hourly wages — Your regular pay for the hours or days you missed
  • Overtime pay — If you regularly worked overtime before the accident, you can claim the overtime you would have earned
  • Bonuses and commissions — Performance bonuses, sales commissions, and incentive pay you lost due to being unable to work
  • Tips and gratuities — For restaurant workers, bartenders, valets, and others who rely on tips as a substantial part of their income
  • Vacation and sick days used — If you burned through your PTO or sick leave to cover your recovery period, those days have a cash value
  • Benefits lost — Health insurance contributions, retirement plan matches, stock options, and other employer-provided benefits, which may be recoverable as part of your compensation package
  • Promotion opportunities missed — A promotion or raise you lost because of your absence may be recoverable if you can show it was reasonably certain, not just possible
  • Self-employment income — Business profits you would have earned if you could have continued working

The key principle is that you should be made whole. Whatever income the accident took from you is recoverable if you can prove the injury caused the loss and show the amount with reasonable certainty — not speculation. This applies whether your injuries came from a car accident, a trucking collision, or a construction site incident.

before: Proving future losses requires expert testimony. A vocational rehabilitation expert can assess what jobs you can and cannot perform given your permanent restrictions. An economist can calculate the present value of your future lost income. Medical experts establish the permanence and extent of your limitations. These experts are especially critical in cases involving catastrophic injuries like those from motorcycle accidents or commercial truck collisions, where victims often face long-term or permanent disabilities.

before: One challenge unique to self-employed workers: the IRS encourages you to deduct every legitimate business expense, which reduces your reported net income. The insurer will point to your tax return and argue that your low reported income means your lost wages are minimal. Your attorney needs to reconstruct your actual earning capacity, not just the number on line 31 of your Schedule C.
after: One challenge unique to self-employed workers: the tax code lets you deduct every legitimate business expense, which reduces your reported net income. The insurer will point to your tax return and argue that your low reported income means your lost wages are minimal. Your attorney needs to reconstruct your actual earning capacity, not just the number on line 31 of your Schedule C.

before: Georgia treats lost wages as a component of compensatory damages under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-12, which allows injured plaintiffs to recover "the full value of the life of the plaintiff" as measured by their ability to earn money. The phrase is broader than it sounds — it covers both past lost wages and diminished future earning capacity.
after: Georgia treats lost wages as special damages — losses that "actually flow from a tortious act" and "must be proved in order to be recovered" (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-2). Wages lost from the date of injury to the date of trial are recoverable when the amount can be determined with reasonable certainty (Dossie v. Sherwood). Lost future earning capacity is a separate item that focuses on permanent or total disability and needs some evidence of what you could earn before and after the injury (Schriever v. Maddox). The loss of your ability to work is also an element of pain and suffering, which the jury values without a fixed formula.

before: If your injury happened on the job, Georgia's workers' compensation system provides wage replacement benefits — typically two-thirds of your average weekly wage, subject to a state-imposed cap. However, if a third party (not your employer) caused or contributed to your injury, you may have both a workers' comp claim and a personal injury claim. The lost wages you can recover through each channel are different, and your workers' comp carrier will likely assert a subrogation lien against any personal injury recovery.
after: If your injury happened on the job, Georgia's workers' compensation system provides wage replacement benefits — typically two-thirds of your average weekly wage, subject to a statutory cap, currently $800 per week. However, if a third party (not your employer) caused or contributed to your injury, you may have both a workers' comp claim and a personal injury claim. The lost wages you can recover through each channel are different, and your workers' comp carrier will likely assert a subrogation lien against any personal injury recovery — though under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-11.1 the carrier can enforce that lien only if your recovery fully and completely compensates you for all of your economic and noneconomic losses, which is why these liens are often negotiated down or defeated.

before: South Carolina allows recovery of lost wages as part of actual or compensatory damages in personal injury actions. The state's common law framework, supplemented by statutes like S.C. Code § 15-38-15 governing joint and several liability, shapes how lost wage claims are handled when multiple defendants share fault.
after: South Carolina allows recovery of lost wages as part of actual or compensatory damages in personal injury actions. The state's common law framework, supplemented by statutes like S.C. Code § 15-38-15 governing joint and several liability, shapes how lost wage claims are handled when multiple defendants share fault.

before: South Carolina uses a modified comparative negligence standard. Your damages are reduced by your percentage of fault, and you are barred from recovery if you are found 51% or more at fault. This is slightly more favorable than Georgia's 50% threshold — a plaintiff who is exactly 50% at fault can still recover in South Carolina but would be barred in Georgia.
after: South Carolina uses a modified comparative negligence standard (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Your damages are reduced by your percentage of fault, and you are barred from recovery if you are found 51% or more at fault. This is slightly more favorable than Georgia's 50% threshold — a plaintiff who is exactly 50% at fault can still recover in South Carolina but would be barred in Georgia.

before: Under S.C. Code § 15-38-15, South Carolina modified the traditional joint and several liability rule. If a defendant is found less than 50% at fault, that defendant is only responsible for their proportionate share of the damages. This affects lost wage recovery when multiple parties contributed to your accident. If one defendant is judgment-proof or uninsured, you may not be able to collect their share of your lost wages from the other defendants.
after: Under S.C. Code § 15-38-15, South Carolina modified the traditional joint and several liability rule. If a defendant is found less than 50% at fault, that defendant is only responsible for their proportionate share of the damages. This affects lost wage recovery when multiple parties contributed to your accident. If one defendant is judgment-proof or uninsured, you may not be able to collect their share of your lost wages from the other defendants. Since January 1, 2026, a defendant can also ask the jury to assign fault to a person who is not a party to the case, which can shrink the share you can collect; a defendant whose conduct was wilful, wanton, reckless or intentional remains liable for the whole award.

before: Both Georgia and South Carolina require injured plaintiffs to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses. If you turned down light-duty work that your doctor approved, or refused treatment that could have shortened your recovery, the insurer will argue your lost wages should be reduced. This does not mean you must accept any job or any treatment — only that your choices must be reasonable under the circumstances.
after: Both Georgia and South Carolina require injured plaintiffs to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses (in Georgia, O.C.G.A. § 51-12-11). If you turned down light-duty work that your doctor approved, or refused treatment that could have shortened your recovery, the insurer will argue your lost wages should be reduced. This does not mean you must accept any job or any treatment — only that your choices must be reasonable under the circumstances.

before: Expert retention. For serious injuries — a traumatic brain injury that affects cognitive function, a spinal cord injury that limits mobility — future earning capacity claims require vocational experts, economists, and life care planners. Your attorney identifies and retains the right experts, coordinates their analyses, and presents their findings in a way that holds up under cross-examination.
